At a body temperature of 30.9 °C [T = 30.9 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate was measured at 66.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 66.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns closely with predictions based on body mass for afrotherian mammals of similar size. Neonates are remarkably small at birth, with newborn individuals weighing approximately 8.1 grams [Wwb = approximately 8.1 grams], a modest mass that reflects the altricial state of the young at parturition. This low birth weight necessitates an extended period of maternal investment, as offspring are entirely dependent on milk during the initial weeks of life. Field observations suggest that this combination of a relatively low metabolic rate and small neonatal mass may represent an adaptive strategy for surviving in the unpredictable, resource-limited environments typical of rocky outcrops and savannah woodlands that the species inhabits across its range.

This reproductive strategy, combining a limited litter size with an extended gestation, appears well suited to the species' ecological niche as a resident of stable but food-limited rocky habitats where high fecundity may be less advantageous than consistent, low-investment offspring production.

This weaning mass represents a substantial increase from the neonatal weight, reflecting a period of rapid somatic growth supported by the mother's milk. Following weaning, juveniles enter a sub-adult phase during which they continue to refine their foraging skills and develop the characteristic saltatorial locomotion of the species. The attainment of a mass approaching adult dimensions occurs over the subsequent weeks, with the weaned young gradually achieving independence from maternal care. This developmental timeline is consistent with the pattern observed in other macroscelidids, where a relatively short lactation period is followed by a prolonged juvenile phase spent learning to capture insect prey in the complex rocky terrain.

This ultimate wet weight places the species at the smaller end of the size spectrum within the genus Elephantulus, with females tending toward slightly larger masses than males in most populations studied to date. The achievement of this adult mass coincides with the full development of the species' characteristic elongated snout and dentition, which are specialised for extracting invertebrates from crevices and leaf litter.

Senescence in older individuals is marked by a gradual decline in locomotor performance and a reduction in the efficiency of insect capture, ultimately leading to natural mortality through a combination of predation and physiological deterioration. The species' ability to persist for several years in the face of environmental stochasticity reflects its adaptation to the stable but low-productivity habitats it occupies across the eastern escarpment of southern Africa, where longevity may confer a selective advantage by allowing multiple reproductive opportunities across variable seasons.
